title: Scalable and interoperable C-V2X framework for real-time intelligent decision support in autonomous mobility
summary: A modular, edge-intelligent mobility operating system (mOS) puts the intersection itself into the control loop: extensible JSON/Protobuf message sets replace rigid SAE J2735 binaries, and a mixed-reality testbed on the KAIST Munji campus lets a real autonomous vehicle negotiate with virtual cars and pedestrians in real time.

paragraphs: Cooperative-ITS research has mostly stopped at simulation or narrow testbeds, and the standardized binary message sets it relies on — SAE J2735, ETSI ITS-G5 — cannot be extended without breaking interoperability with devices already in the field. The road, meanwhile, still carries human-driven cars, pedestrians and micromobility that broadcast nothing at all, so a vehicle reasoning from connected data alone never sees the whole intersection.

This study proposes the mobility operating system (mOS): a plug-and-play, edge-intelligent framework in which the intersection interprets traffic and issues speed advice, validated on a mixed-reality testbed where a physical connected autonomous vehicle interacts with virtual agents in real time. Published in Communications in Transportation Research, with Prof. Inhi Kim as a corresponding author.

sections.heading: Infrastructure in the control loop
sections.body: Rather than making each vehicle smarter in isolation, mOS gives the intersection edge the deciding role. A reservation-based autonomous intersection management scheme (after Dresner and Stone) is extended so that the requesting vehicle's maximum speed is updated dynamically: the edge finds the space–time cell each approaching vehicle would occupy and returns a recommended speed for every timestamp. The vehicle's Apollo stack accepts the suggestion through ROS and CAN/BUS only when it poses no collision risk, so infrastructure guidance never overrides on-board safety.

sections.heading: Messages that can grow
sections.body: The message set is deliberately minimal — a mandatory timestamp plus application-specific fields, serialized as JSON or Protobuf — so new services can be added without renegotiating a binary schema. Transport is hybrid: gRPC carries compressed, field-name-free messages for time-critical commands that need acknowledgement, while RabbitMQ handles periodic best-effort data such as GPS updates. A Kubernetes-based system orchestrator monitors network and resource metrics, scales services horizontally when traffic surges, and lets neighbouring intersections hand over or offload computation instead of routing everything through a central cloud.

sections.heading: A testbed that is half virtual
sections.body: Experiments ran at a four-leg unsignalized intersection on the KAIST Munji campus in Daejeon, with 3.5 m lanes meeting the Euro NCAP recommendation and a controllable signal box switched off. The connected vehicle was a Hyundai Tucson Hybrid NX4 carrying a Novatel PwrPak7 GNSS receiver and an Epson G320 IMU (RTK-corrected, 100 Hz, 0.05 m deviation) plus a commercial 5G router. A metaverse server synchronizes virtual vehicles, a driving simulator and a pedestrian simulator into the same scene, so a person can step into the path of a real moving car with no physical risk.

sections.heading: Guided crossings are smoother
sections.body: Two scenarios were compared with and without speed suggestions. Mean post-encroachment time (PET) fell from 5.99 s (SD 0.77) to 4.62 s (SD 1.10) for vehicle-to-vehicle interaction, and from 2.94 s (SD 0.93) to 1.76 s (SD 1.20) for vehicle-to-pedestrian interaction — shorter but also less variable gaps, indicating more predictable negotiation. Without guidance the vehicle read a jaywalking pedestrian as a hazard, braked abruptly and stopped mid-path; with guidance it crossed without stopping, while every guided PET stayed above the 1.0 s safety threshold.

sections.heading: Real-time, with caveats
sections.body: Mean end-to-end latency was 48.46 ms (SD 63.62 ms, max 479.39 ms) and mean jitter 60.17 ms, with packet loss between 0.106% and 0.285% across approach speeds of 20–50 km/h — low enough for real-time speed advice, but with occasional spikes that would threaten safety-critical exchanges. The trials used a commercial 5G router rather than dedicated C-V2X infrastructure, so dedicated PC5 links should tighten these numbers; a head-to-head comparison against existing V2X systems and scaling across multiple intersections remain future work.

title: Audio-Visual Synergistic Role in Promoting Active Travel
summary: A multi-scale, explainable machine-learning framework using 2.79 million Shenzhen bikeshare trips shows that street soundscapes — not just streetscapes — shape cycling demand, with audio-visual synergies revealing high-leverage, low-cost design levers for active travel.

paragraphs: Cycling is central to sustainable, human-centric mobility, yet bikeshare usage stays low even where the macro-scale built environment is favorable. Drawing on 2.79 million dockless bikeshare trips in Shenzhen, China, this study asks whether the fine-grained things riders hear and see — soundscapes and streetscapes read from street-view imagery — also shape where people ride.

A multi-scale, explainable machine-learning framework (LightGBM with SHAP and Accumulated Local Effects) quantifies each dimension's contribution, its nonlinear thresholds, and the synergy between what a street sounds like and what it looks like.

sections.heading: Hearing the street, not just seeing it
sections.body: Earlier street-view studies quantified how a place looks — greenery, sky, perceived beauty — but ignored how it sounds. Eight soundscape indicators (intensity, quality, traffic/natural/mechanical sources, and pleasant-chaotic-eventful emotions) are derived alongside six streetscape indicators, then validated against on-site sound-level-meter readings at 72 points, reaching a moderately strong agreement (r = 0.60).

sections.heading: Sound outweighs sight
sections.body: Adding audio-visual perception lifts explained variance from R² = 0.40 (built environment only) to 0.60. The built environment still dominates (55.5%), but among the micro-scale cues the soundscape (24.7%) carries more weight than the visual streetscape (19.8%) — the first evidence that what riders hear can matter more than what they see. Natural sound, pleasantness, and sound quality are the strongest auditory drivers.

sections.heading: Effects that bend, not rise forever
sections.body: The explainable model reveals thresholds rather than straight lines. Cycling responds to subway access only within about 1 km, and bus density turns supportive past roughly 42 stops/km². Pleasant sound, sound quality, and natural sound help only up to a moderate level (≈ 0.5–0.6) and then reverse — pristine quiet often marks remote, low-demand areas.

sections.heading: When sound and sight work together
sections.body: The dimensions interact. High sound quality boosts cycling only where a street is not boring and also looks beautiful — quality alone is not enough. Natural sound and perceived safety reinforce each other strongly, creating calm, low-stress riding environments, though natural sound paired with visible affluence produces no such lift, since wealthier areas simply cycle less.

sections.heading: Design for the ear, not only the eye
sections.body: Because these sensory qualities are cheap to adjust relative to heavy infrastructure, they offer high-leverage levers: noise barriers and absorptive or vegetative screens, pleasant sound-masking, and safer, livelier street furniture. Planners should target places where audio and visual quality are mismatched, and tune each perception within its effective range rather than maximizing it.

title: Traffic demand modeling using agent model
summary: Building a digital twin of road traffic with agent-based simulation (2022~2025): macroscopic transport simulation is integrated with activity-based modeling to reproduce realistic traffic flows and predict traffic volumes at the micro-analysis-zone level.

paragraphs: Development of a digital twin for road traffic using autonomous driving Level 4/4+ big data (2022~2025). A multi-scale traffic simulation space identical to the real world enables the analysis and prediction of situations that are infeasible to test in reality, such as future mixed traffic environments.

The macroscopic stage generates realistic traffic flows by producing origin-destination data at the MAZ (Micro Analysis Zone) level and predicting traffic volumes for each route. The generated data feeds the microscopic stage, where an activity-based model (ABM) dynamically reproduces individual travel behavior at the coordinate level.

sections.heading: Integrated simulation platform
bullets: Simulation manager data system and custom configuration schemes that generate result data tailored to the user's analytical purpose
Vehicle generation methodologies defining generation intervals, lane assignment priorities, and initial speeds to reproduce realistic traffic flows
OD matrix recalculation and simulation settings such as vehicle mix rates to support macroscopic policy analysis

sections.heading: Validation against empirical data
bullets: Predicted traffic demand from the activity-based model is verified against mobile-based metropolitan movement data
Predicted traffic volumes are validated against real traffic counts at VDS stations, achieving a GEH-based accuracy of 90.48%

title: Real-time Prediction-based Conflict Measures for Evaluating Pedestrian Crossing Safety
summary: A unified prediction-driven pedestrian-vehicle safety evaluation approach for intelligent intersections, integrating deep learning-based behavior prediction with traffic conflict measures to evaluate pedestrian crossing risk in real time.

paragraphs: The overall objective is a unified prediction-driven pedestrian-vehicle safety evaluation approach for intelligent intersections. Deep learning-based behavior prediction is integrated with traffic conflict measures to enable real-time evaluation of potential and future pedestrian crossing risks across different intersection scenarios, from individual interactions to crowd crossings.

sections.heading: Deterministic conflict evaluation at non-signalized intersections
sections.body: Pedestrian and vehicle time-to-arrival are predicted with deterministic deep learning motion models, formulating the Predicted Lane-based Time-to-Collision (PLTTC) and benchmarking it against TTC, MTTC, and PET. Published in Transportation Research Interdisciplinary Perspectives (2025).

sections.heading: Probabilistic conflict evaluation under behavioral uncertainty
sections.body: Probabilistic trajectories generated with mixture-Gaussian model outputs yield the Stochastic Predicted Time-to-Collision (SPTTC) for early-stage conflict identification with high-variability pedestrian behavior. In revision at IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems.

sections.heading: Real-time crash risk at signalized intersections
sections.body: Deep learning-derived conflict information (Predicted Lane-based Gap Time) is integrated into Extreme Value Theory crash-risk estimation, comparing four EVT formulations against conventional conflict measures. In revision at Analytic Methods in Accident Research.

sections.heading: Crowd crossing risk evaluation
sections.body: Collective pedestrian dynamics are learned with multi-agent trajectory prediction, and a Crowd Gap Time (C-GT) measure evaluates pedestrian-vehicle risk during crowd crossings against baselines such as the Social Force Model. Ongoing.

sections.heading: Behavioral validation with VR and EEG
sections.body: Virtual reality experiments with electroencephalography responses test whether prediction-based conflict measures reflect human-perceived crossing risk and can guide threshold calibration. Ongoing.

title: Human-centric traffic safety
summary: Investigating how drivers, pedestrians, and evacuees make decisions in safety-critical mobility situations through immersive VR experiments, covering micromobility safety, pedestrian-ADAS interaction, and underground/rail environments.

paragraphs: A long-running line of work using immersive VR experiments to measure how drivers, pedestrians, and evacuees actually decide, attend, and move in safety-critical mobility situations. Controlled virtual environments reproduce realistic urban roadways, school zones, tunnels, and subway stations while capturing behavior that would be unsafe or impossible to observe in the field.

sections.heading: Micromobility safety and driver behavior
sections.body: How a driver's own riding experience shapes overtaking maneuvers, lateral distance, and risk-taking around bicycles and e-scooters in mixed traffic, studied with VR-based driving simulators (Transportation Research Part F, 2026).

sections.heading: Pedestrian safety and ADAS
sections.body: How the presentation of safety information — a real-time count of crossing pedestrians, or a UWB-based pedestrian tag — changes braking behavior, cognitive load, and the safety margins drivers leave under uncertainty (Accident Analysis & Prevention, 2024).

sections.heading: Underground and rail safety
sections.body: VR studies of pedestrian evacuation route choice during subway-station fires, in-tunnel information design under varying lighting and speed limits (Tunnelling and Underground Space Technology, 2025), and how age-related perceptual constraints reshape transport disadvantage in railway information systems.

images.caption: Immersive VR experiment platform: Cyberith Virtualizer Elite 2 omnidirectional treadmill with HTC Vive Pro 2 and Unity 3D

title: Analysis Public Transport Accessibility
summary: A comparative framework that measures the gap between planned transit schedules (GTFS) and actual smart-card usage with an extended G2SFCA accessibility model, diagnosing where public transport supply and real travel demand diverge.

paragraphs: Many cities face a spatial mismatch where public transport supply is rigidly misaligned with real-world travel demand, leading to service inefficiency and transportation inequality. This research develops a comparative framework that analyzes the gap between planned transit schedules (GTFS) and actual passenger usage (smart-card OD data) with an extended spatial accessibility model, providing quantitative evidence of where transit resources are wasted or lacking — particularly during off-peak hours.

sections.heading: Extended G2SFCA methodology
sections.body: Diverse services are integrated into a single supply metric using gross floor area, and door-to-door accessibility combines walking and in-vehicle travel times with a Gaussian decay function — moving beyond binary catchment measurements toward a more realistic accessibility index.

sections.heading: Realization rate analysis
sections.body: GTFS supply and smart-card usage are matched at the stop level, and a regression-based realization rate quantifies how far the plan is implemented in reality: alignment is high during peak hours but efficiency drops significantly at midday.

sections.heading: Spatio-temporal mismatch
sections.body: Geographically Weighted Regression reveals a structural midday discrepancy near northern industrial areas of Daejeon — routes rigidly centered on commuting fail to serve midday lifestyle travel such as shopping and medical care — while western and eastern residential clusters use transit efficiently.

sections.heading: Policy implication
sections.body: Transit policy should align the destinations of supply and demand rather than simply increase supply volume, spatially reallocating surplus capacity from low-realization routes to active residential and commercial areas.

images.caption: GWR local coefficients for planned supply vs. realized usage in Daejeon (AM / midday / PM)
Analysis pipeline: data sources, preprocessing, accessibility calculation, and spatial analysis in ArcGIS Pro

title: Remote Autonomous Driving: Tele-driving Between Daejeon and Jeju
summary: A live tele-driving demonstration controlling a driverless shuttle on Jeju Island from KAIST's Daejeon campus over 415 km, using ultra-low-latency network federated communication to relay live video and control commands without delay.

paragraphs: Fully autonomous driving still struggles with unexpected situations and complex road environments. Tele-driving offers a complementary alternative for the current transition period: a remote operator controls the vehicle in real time while retaining the ability to communicate with onboard passengers, enabling safer responses in unforeseen situations.

In 2025, TUPA and its collaborators demonstrated this at scale — remotely operating a driverless shuttle located on Jeju Island from the KAIST campus in Daejeon, a physical distance of 415 km. The work was carried out with Toronto EMG and KAIST, combining wired and wireless network communication technologies for both external (vehicle-to-remote) and internal vehicle communication.

sections.heading: Ultra-low-latency remote control
sections.body: Safe remote control of an autonomous vehicle requires ultra-precise software and real-time communication. The team's remote-control interface processes data in real time while maintaining stability, and an ultra-low-latency network carried live driving footage and control commands between Daejeon and Jeju without perceptible delay during real-world road testing.

sections.heading: Network federated technology
sections.body: For the first time, network federated technology was applied to remote driving, demonstrating seamless mobility communication across the wide-area link and bringing remote-controlled autonomous vehicles closer to everyday deployment.

sections.heading: Toward commercial services in restricted spaces
sections.body: If commercialized, tele-driving services are expected to first appear in limited, controlled spaces such as airports, ports, and logistics facilities, and as a mobility option for passengers with restricted destinations — part of a broader vision for mobility that is safer, smarter, and more human.

title: Goal-Driven Experimental Pipeline for Multi-Vehicle Autonomous Driving in CARLA in ROS2
summary: A CARLA-ROS2 experimental pipeline for goal-driven autonomous driving on Lanelet2 maps, composing multi-vehicle scenarios that mix custom driving policies with rule-based autopilot vehicles to study interaction-aware driving behaviors.

paragraphs: Autonomous driving research increasingly emphasizes interaction among multiple vehicles rather than isolated ego-centric driving, yet controlled experiments mixing heterogeneous vehicle behaviors remain difficult without a unified, goal-driven experimental pipeline.

This research constructs a CARLA-ROS2 pipeline that enables goal-driven autonomous driving using Lanelet2 lane-level maps. Vehicles can be controlled either by custom driving policies or by CARLA's built-in autopilot, supporting flexible composition of multi-vehicle scenarios with varying ratios of autonomous and autopilot-driven vehicles — a foundation for studying interaction-aware driving behaviors, priority decision policies, and future V2X-based coordination.

sections.heading: Core capabilities
bullets: Lanelet2-based goal-driven driving experiments using lane-level map information
Multi-vehicle scenario composition with heterogeneous driving policies
Controlled evaluation of interaction-aware driving behavior under structured map and goal conditions
Modular ROS2 architecture enabling sim-to-real extension
Extensible toward V2X information sharing and priority-based decision policies, including learning-based policies (end-to-end, RL)

images.caption: End-to-end autonomous driving demonstration using CARLA-ROS2 integration, visualized in RViz alongside CARLA

title: VR Driving Simulator Platform
summary: An integrated platform combining VISSIM traffic microsimulation, a driving simulator, virtual reality, and Python to study connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic — the shared hardware and software base behind TUPA's human-in-the-loop driving studies.

paragraphs: TUPA develops an architecture that ties together VISSIM microsimulation, a physical driving simulator rig, virtual reality, and Python-based control and analysis code, so that vehicle dynamics, driver behavior, and surrounding traffic can all be represented within one framework.

The platform is the common foundation behind the lab's overtaking-behavior and metaverse co-simulation studies, and is intended to help develop and validate techniques for improving traffic congestion, safety, and network performance under connected and automated driving.

images.caption: PTV VISSIM traffic microsimulation linked to Unity, driven through a VR headset and a force-feedback wheel and pedal set

title: Metaverse-Based Emerging Technology: Unity–VISSIM Co-simulation
summary: A co-simulation environment linking PTV VISSIM's traffic microsimulation with a Unity 3D virtual environment, enabling human-in-the-loop testing with a VR headset and a force-feedback driving wheel and pedals.

paragraphs: TUPA builds a metaverse-based testbed that couples PTV VISSIM's traffic microsimulation engine with a Unity 3D virtual environment, so a human driver can be placed inside a live simulated traffic stream rather than only observing it from the outside.

The environment combines a VR headset with a force-feedback driving wheel and pedals so surrounding VISSIM-driven traffic can be experienced first-hand. A multi-agent version of this metaverse platform was exhibited at the 2023 Seoul Mobility Show, and it underpins a KAIST-funded testbed project on mixed traffic control strategies.

images.caption: VISSIM (large-scale traffic simulation) and Unity (3D virtual environment) co-simulation, paired with a VR headset (2880×1600, 90Hz, 110° FOV) and a force-feedback driving wheel and pedal set

title: Human Factor Safety: Interactive Driving Behavior in Overtaking Situations
summary: Using the multi-agent driving simulator platform, this line of work studies how a human driver negotiates overtaking maneuvers around a slower vehicle while oncoming traffic is present.

paragraphs: Overtaking is one of the highest-risk maneuvers in mixed traffic, requiring a driver to judge oncoming traffic, closing speed, and the slower vehicle's behavior at the same time. TUPA studies this interaction with its multi-agent driving simulator, which puts a human driver behind the wheel of the overtaking vehicle while other agents control the oncoming and low-speed vehicles.

This line of work spans several studies led by Taeho Oh — from early two-lane two-way road overtaking maneuvers (ITS World Congress 2022), to machine-learning-supported robust overtaking behavior (TRB 2023), to safe overtaking behavior thresholds under human interaction (TRB 2024).

images.caption: Multi-agent driving simulator pipeline (human interaction, data collection, machine learning, communication interface, analysis) for the overtaking-vehicle / oncoming-vehicle scenario

title: Data-Driven Traffic Volume Imputation from Multi-Source Data Collection
summary: Combining Roadside Equipment (RSE) probe data with Vehicle Detection System (VDS) loop-detector counts, this research imputes and predicts traffic volume across a road network using graph-based deep learning — a practical, data-driven approach to real-world transportation operation.

paragraphs: Neither data source alone covers the full network: RSE units report real-time speed, travel time, and sample counts along road segments, while VDS loop detectors report volume, speed, and occupancy at fixed points. Representing the road network as a graph lets a deep learning model fuse both sources and impute traffic volume at links with sparse or missing sensor data, evaluated against historical monthly, weekly, and daily traffic patterns.

Led by Donghyun Kwon, published as "Large-Scale Network Imputation and Prediction of Traffic Volume Based on Multi-Source Data Collection System" (Transportation Research Record, 2023) and "Large Scale Multi-Source Traffic Flow Forecasting Based on Attention-Based Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks–LSTM" (ITS World Congress 2022).

images.caption: RSE and VDS data collection at road-segment/link level, represented as a graph and compared across monthly, weekly, and daily historical periods

title: Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Optimization
summary: A Neighbor Dueling Deep Q-Network (NDDQN) jointly controls four neighboring intersections, choosing signal actions that reduce vehicle emissions rather than only minimizing delay.

paragraphs: Conventional signal control optimizes each intersection in isolation and typically rewards shorter delay or queue length. This work instead controls four neighboring intersections simultaneously with a Neighbor Dueling Deep Q-Network, so each agent's signal decisions account for traffic conditions at adjacent intersections, using reduced emissions — not just travel time — as the reward signal.

Led by Jaeeun Jung, published as "EcoMRL: Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Control for Urban Air Quality" (International Journal of Sustainable Transportation, 2024) and filed as a Korean patent, "Reinforcement Learning-Based Signal Control Method and System Considering Environmental Impact" (2024).
